answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1667–1745 · Anglo-Irish satirist, essayist & Dean of St Patrick’s, Dublin
answer.sourceLine: A genuine Swift line from his aphorism collection “Thoughts on Various Subjects” (the “Various Thoughts, Moral and Diverting” dated 1 October 1706, first printed 1711). Two independent full-text editions preserve the exact wording, “We have just enough Religion to make us hate, but not enough to make us love one another.”

source.excerpt: We have just enough Religion to make us hate, but not enough to make us love one another.
trail: The Jonathan Swift Archive ↗ prints the line verbatim in “Various Thoughts, Moral and Diverting,” dated 1 October 1706, noting editions of 1711, 1727 and 1735.
The full text at Quotidiana ↗ carries the identical sentence within “Thoughts on Various Subjects.”
WIST Quotations ↗ sources the line to Swift’s “Thoughts on Various Subjects” (1706).
source.excerptNote: One aphorism among dozens in the collection; the wording is stable across the 1711, 1727 and 1735 printings.

author.name: Jonathan Swift
author.heading: About Jonathan Swift
author.bio: Jonathan Swift was an Anglo-Irish satirist, poet, and Anglican clergyman who became Dean of St Patrick’s Cathedral in Dublin. Best known for Gulliver’s Travels (1726) and the savage essay A Modest Proposal (1729), he was also a prolific author of short aphorisms — terse moral observations of the kind that produced this line on religion and human enmity.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Swift is correct — but the wording is frequently clipped in quote databases.

items.why: Many sites — e.g. BrainyQuote ↗ and Quotefancy ↗ — drop the word “just” and render it “We have enough religion to make us hate…,” which is not Swift’s printed text.

misattribution.truthLine: The author is genuinely Swift; the authentic wording keeps the word “just”: “We have just enough Religion to make us hate…,” as the Jonathan Swift Archive ↗ preserves it.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: Swift wrote the line as a compact aphorism among dozens in “Thoughts on Various Subjects,” a genre he excelled at: a single sentence that turns a whole argument on its hinge. Here the target is sectarian enmity — the observation that partial, formal religion can inflame hatred while stopping short of the charity that would dissolve it.
Coming from a satirist who was himself a senior Anglican cleric, the epigram has kept its bite for three centuries and is quoted in debates over religious conflict to this day.
